text: Florence Ann Farmer (24 January 1873 – 26 June 1958) was a pioneering woman in politics in Stoke on Trent, Staffordshire, England, becoming the first female councillor on the county borough council and later the first female Lord Mayor of the city in 1931–32. She was one of the children of George and Mary Farmer, born in Longton, Staffordshire, and her father, George, was an active Liberal local politician who served as secretary of the local party, a Justice of the Peace, and mayor of Longton from 1895 to 1896. After leaving school, Farmer trained as a teacher and served as headmistress of Uttoxeter Road Girls School in Longton from 1895 to 1906. She resigned from teaching to co-found the Phoenix Steam Laundry company with her brother George, and after his death in 1917, continued the business with his widow, Maude, until 1927 when Maude retired, leaving Florence in charge. Farmer was a founding member of the National Federation of Launderers and became the first woman to sit on its national executive committee. Women could only be elected to the local board of guardians since the Local Government Act 1894, and it was not until 1907 that women were allowed to serve on borough councils under the Qualification of Women (County and Borough Councils) Act 1907. Initially a Liberal, Farmer shifted to socialism and joined the Labour Party after the end of the First World War. In 1915, she was elected to the County Borough of Stoke on Trent board of guardians, and in November 1919, she became the first woman elected to the Stoke-on-Trent Council, winning unopposed for No. 23 ward (Longton). She served on various committees, including the watch committee, where she proposed the appointment of women constables; although initially defeated, the proposal was later accepted, leading to the first women constables in Stoke being appointed in 1921. Appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1920, she became the first woman to be made an Alderman of the City of Stoke-on-Trent in 1928. She chaired the local Labour Party branch from 1929 to 1931. When Lady Cynthia Mosley, the MP for Stoke-on-Trent, resigned from the Labour Party in 1931 to join her husband Oswald Mosley’s New Party, Farmer was nominated as the Labour candidate but was not selected; the nomination went to Ellis Smith. In October 1931, she was unanimously chosen to be Lord Mayor of Stoke-on-Trent for 1932–33, becoming the first woman to hold the office and only the fourth woman in England to serve as a Lord Mayor. At her investiture in November 1931, she wore the same mayoral chains that her father had worn as mayor of Longton in 1895. Farmer remained on the city council until 1945 and was granted the Freedom of the City in 1946. She never married and died in June 1958 at the age of 85.
